title: What the research tells us
summary: Explain why we observe, reflect, try and check again.

sections.heading: Your outcome
sections.html:
Explain why we observe, reflect, try and check again.

Estimated reading time; check at your own pace. This is developmental support, separate from qualifications and formal assessment.

sections.heading: Start with the child
sections.html: Mentoring helps an adult coach make one useful change and notice what it does for the children. We use observation, reflection, specific feedback and another attempt. Intent over outcome is our coaching value: recognise a purposeful decision even when execution is unsuccessful. It is not an empirical feedback-effect claim.

sections.heading: Findings and limits
sections.html: Raabe and colleagues (2019) reviewed interventions with PE teachers and youth-sport coaches. Their review suggests support can change adult behaviour; it does not validate our Hub or a particular visit length. Haugan and colleagues (2021) studied a Norwegian coach-mentoring programme. Coach and athlete perceptions did not consistently agree. This setting and self-report evidence cannot establish effects for grassroots U6–U8 children. Feeling more confident is useful information, but does not demonstrate better practice or player experience.

sections.heading: Our proposed application
sections.html: Agree one coach behaviour, observe what happens, let the coach interpret it, and test an achievable change. Ask what would count as an unhelpful result. If it does not help, adapt the idea rather than blame the coach. Psychological safety here means making it possible to ask for help and discuss mistakes without humiliation; safeguarding duties still apply.

sections.heading: Optional mentor guidance
sections.html: FIFA’s student-coach example illustrates a pre-brief, agreed observation and reflective feedback in a licence-assessment setting. We adapt the conversation for development, separate from formal assessment. A successful playing career does not replace preparation in listening, questioning, feedback and boundaries. Practise describing an event before offering advice.

quiz.prompt: A coach feels more confident after the visit. What can we conclude?
options: Mentoring has improved the children’s learning.
Confidence changed; we still need to observe practice and player experience.
quiz.explanation: Confidence and observed practice are different outcomes; ask what the children experienced.

quiz.prompt: A former professional player volunteers as a mentor. What preparation is needed?
options: Only a longer list of drills.
Prepare listening, feedback, supervision and hand-back boundaries.
quiz.explanation: Playing knowledge may help, but does not establish mentoring skill.

quiz.prompt: The first experiment does not help. What next?
options: Review observations with the coach and adapt one thing.
Record success because the visit happened.
Insist on the same approach indefinitely.
quiz.explanation: An unhelpful attempt is information for the next decision, not proof the coach failed.

takeaway: Choose one coaching behaviour and describe what the children might experience differently.
